newsitem.title: CHINA: Peasants weep while leaders plot over Deng's body.
newsitem.headline: Peasants weep while leaders plot over Deng's body.

text.p: Wailing and falling to their knees, several thousand unruly mourners swamped Deng Xiaoping's birthplace on Friday, while in Beijing leaders began political shadow plays around the body of the Chinese patriarch.
Armed police were summoned to keep order in Paifang village in remote southwest Sichuan province where pilgrims with tear-streaked faces prostrated themselves on the ground.
"There are a lot of people crying, some of them young, but most of them are older," said an official at Deng's former residence, now a museum.
"Some old people have knelt on the ground and are crying. Their faces are covered in tears."
Deng, chief architect of market-oriented reforms that transformed China into a rising superpower, died on Wednesday night aged 92.
There have been few public displays of emotion over Deng's death in a country seemingly too absorbed with new material pursuits to grieve.
Shrouded in secrecy, leaders in the capital plotted over details of Deng's funeral and their own careers.
The funeral will be a simple farewell: no overseas dignitaries, no foreign media, no lying in state -- and no tomb.
Deng's corneas will be donated to an eye bank, his body offered for medical dissection and his ashes scattered into the sea according to his wishes.

Political analysts said the size of a 459-strong funeral committee led by Deng protege Jiang Zemin hinted at arcane succession politics unchanged since the days when emperors ruled from the Dragon Throne of Beijing's Forbidden City.
By packing the committee with a political "who's who", the leadership was trying to send a signal of unity.
It also served to mask internal Communist Party machinations as key figures jockeyed for position before the 15th party congress next October when top posts and policies will be revealed.
An elite group might have displayed too hastily who is in and who is out.

In imperial China, social convulsions often accompanied the transfer of the "mandate of heaven" to a new emperor. While the latest power shift so far has been seamless, the analysts said later upheavals were possible.

Jiang, 70, must now confront his own mortality and defuse challenges from other aspirants to power, among them Qiao Shi, the former security tsar who now heads parliament, economic supremo Zhu Rongji and premier Li Peng. Shadowy figures as yet unknown in the outside world could be lurking in the wings.

"Jiang Zemin, who while Deng Xiaoping was alive was the young successor, has become at the moment of Deng's death the incumbent leader who is immediately faced with a succession crisis," said Australian sinologist Geremie Barme.
Barme added that by monopolising the three main arms of power -- state presidency, head of the Communist Party and armed forces chief -- Jiang may have stretched himself too far.
Taiwan state television quoted President Lee Teng-hui as saying in Taipei that he was "not optimistic" about Jiang's succession. It did not elaborate.
China's propaganda machine went into overdrive, hailing diminutive Deng as a giant whose stature could never be matched and pledging the army's loyalty to his political heirs.
As flags around the capital flew at half-mast on the second day of official mourning, authorities sounded a cautious note with calls for stability.
Security was discreet in the capital and the atmosphere calm. People hurried to work as usual on a bright and crisp Friday morning.
"Comrade Deng Xiaoping... became a great son of the people, a giant who will never be matched," the People's Daily said in a commentary. "The people of the motherland love and esteem him."
Asian leaders sounded more glowing tributes to Deng.
Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew said Deng's spirit and courage had never failed and he had helped set the stage for China to become a superpower.
"He saved China. Without him, China could have been like the Soviet Union. Instead China will become a huge heavyweight nation in 30 years," Lee wrote to Jiang.
Financial experts ruled out any immediate hiccups for the burgeoning economy following the demise of a man whose "open door" policies spawned foreign investment zones and revived the stock market.
"I am optimistic on the economy," said Lin Qingsong, an economist at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. "Overall, we are in a very good situation economically."
China chalked up growth of 9.7 percent last year and held once troublesome inflation to 6 percent, well below target and down sharply from more than 14 percent in 1995.

Other economists said reforms were unlikely to gather pace in the uncertain months before the party congress. But China had enough of an economic cushion that it could bide its time as it charted future change.
"The Chinese have the luxury of being able to go ahead slowly," said an economist.
